p.src: Now Lu Zhishen crossed several hillsides and came upon a great pine forest and a mountain path. Following the mountain path, he had gone less than half a li when he looked up and saw a dilapidated temple, its bells and chimes ringing in the wind. At the temple gate hung an old vermilion signboard bearing four gold characters, now all faded, which read: “Temple of the Earthen Jar.” After another forty or fifty paces, he crossed a stone bridge and saw before him an ancient temple, clearly of great age. Entering through the gate and looking carefully around, he found that although it was a great monastery, it was grievously ruined. This was what he saw:

p.src: The bell tower had fallen, and the temple halls lay in ruins. The temple gate was thick with grey-green moss; the scripture repository was overgrown with emerald lichen. Reed shoots pierced the knees of Shakyamuni Buddha, as though he were still upon the Snowy Mountains; Thorns twined about Guanyin’s body, as if she still kept watch upon Fragrant Mountain. The heavenly guardians were broken, and birds nested in their bosoms; Indra leaned askew, while spiders spun webs inside his mouth. Headless arhats—their sacred bodies too had suffered calamity; Arm-broken vajra guardians—what use now were their supernatural powers? Rabbit holes hid within the monastery kitchen, and fox tracks marked the Dragon-Flower Terrace.

p.src: After entering the temple, Lu Zhishen made straight for the guest prefect’s quarters. But the great doors before the quarters were gone, and the surrounding walls had completely fallen away. Zhishen thought, “How did such a great temple fall into this state?” He went straight to the abbot’s quarters. The ground there was covered with swallow droppings, and the door was secured with a lock thickly draped in cobwebs. Zhishen planted his priest’s staff in the ground and called, “A traveling monk has come to beg a meal!” He called for a long while, but no one answered. Returning to inspect the monastery kitchen, he found that even the pots were gone and the stoves had all collapsed. Zhishen took off his bundle and set it before the guardian of the refectory, then raised his staff and went searching everywhere. Behind the kitchen he found a small room where several old monks sat upon the floor, every one of them sallow and wasted. Zhishen bellowed, “You monks have no manners at all! I called and called, yet not one of you answered.” The monks waved their hands and said, “Do not speak so loudly.” Zhishen said, “I am a traveling monk asking for a meal. What danger can there be in that?” An old monk replied, “We ourselves have had nothing in our bellies for three days. Where could we find food for you?” Zhishen said, “I am a monk from Mount Wutai. Even some gruel will do—give me half a bowl.” The old monk said, “Since you are a monk from the abode of living buddhas, it is only right that we should feed you. But the monks of our temple have scattered, and not a single grain remains for alms food. We old monks truly have been starving for three days.” Zhishen said, “Nonsense! I do not believe a great place like this has no food for the monks.” The old monk said, “This was once no insignificant place. But because it was a public monastery open to monks from all quarters, a wandering monk came here with a Taoist and took charge of it; then they ruined everything the monastery possessed. There is no evil those two will not commit, and they drove all the monks away. A few of us old ones could not walk far, so we had no choice but to remain here; that is why we have nothing to eat.” Zhishen said, “Nonsense! What harm can one monk and one Taoist possibly do? Why did you not report them to the authorities?” The old monk said, “Master, you do not understand. The government offices are far from here, and even government troops cannot restrain them. That monk and Taoist are fearsome men, both killers and incendiaries. They now make their lair in a place behind the abbot’s quarters.” Zhishen asked, “What are those two called?” The old monk replied, “The monk’s surname is Cui, his religious name is Daocheng, and his nickname is ‘Iron Buddha’; The Taoist’s surname is Qiu, he is known as Little Second, and his nickname is ‘Flying Yaksha.’ Neither of them resembles a man of religion. They are no different from brigands of the greenwood, merely using the outward guise of holy men to shelter themselves.” While Zhishen was still questioning them, he suddenly caught a fragrant smell. Staff in hand, Zhishen went round to the rear to investigate. There he saw an earthen stove covered by a lid of woven grass, with clouds of steam escaping through it. When Zhishen lifted the lid, he found a pot of millet gruel cooking inside. Zhishen cursed, “You old monks have no decency! You said you had eaten nothing for three days, yet here is a whole pot of gruel cooking. Why should men of religion tell lies?” When Zhishen discovered their gruel, the old monks cried out in dismay and snatched away all the bowls, plates, alms bowls, ladles, and buckets. Zhishen was hungry and could not help wanting the gruel, but had no vessel to use. Then he noticed beside the stove a broken lacquered offering stand with nothing but dust upon it. Seeing it, Zhishen found wit in desperation: he leaned his staff aside, picked up a handful of straw by the stove, and wiped the dust from the stand; Then he lifted the pot with both hands and poured all the gruel onto the stand.

p.src: The old monks all rushed forward to snatch some gruel, but Zhishen sent each of them sprawling with a shove; some fell, while others fled. Zhishen then scooped up the gruel in his hands and ate it. He had eaten only a few mouthfuls when the old monk said, “We truly have had nothing to eat for three days. We only just begged that little millet and made some rough gruel from it, yet now you are eating ours as well.” After five or seven mouthfuls, Zhishen heard this and abandoned the gruel without eating any more. Just then he heard someone outside singing a ribald song. Zhishen washed his hands, took up his staff, and went out to look. Through a gap in the ruined wall he saw a Taoist wearing a black headcloth, a cloth jacket, a multicolored sash about his waist, and hemp sandals on his feet. He carried a shoulder pole; from a bamboo basket at one end protruded several fish tails, beside some meat laid on lotus leaves; At the other end he carried a jar of wine, likewise covered with lotus leaves. p.src: The old monks hurried out, waved their hands, and quietly pointed him out to Zhishen, saying, “That Daoist is Qiu Xiaoyi, the Flying Yaksha.” Once they had pointed him out, Zhishen raised his monk’s staff and followed after him. Unaware that Zhishen was following behind, the Daoist walked straight through the wall behind the abbot’s quarters. Zhishen followed him inside at once. Looking around, he saw a table set beneath a green locust tree, laid with several dishes, three wine cups, and three pairs of chopsticks. In the middle sat a fat monk, with eyebrows like strokes of black lacquer and a face as dark as ink; his whole body bulged with coarse flesh, and his black belly showed below his chest. A young woman sat to one side. The Daoist set down his bamboo basket and took a seat as well. Zhishen strode up before them. The monk started in alarm, sprang to his feet, and said, “Please sit down, brother, and share a cup with us.” Holding up his monk’s staff, Zhishen demanded, “How did you two come to ruin this temple?” The monk replied, “Please sit down, brother, and hear what this humble monk has to say.” Zhishen glared at him and said, “Speak! Speak!” The monk said, “Formerly this temple was a splendid place, with broad estates and a great multitude of monks. But those old monks beneath the cloister drank wine, ran riot, and spent temple money keeping women. When the abbot tried in vain to restrain them, they brought false accusations against him and drove him out. That is how the whole temple fell into ruin. All the monks dispersed, and the lands have already been sold. This Daoist and I have only lately come to take charge of the place, intending to restore the monastery and rebuild its halls.” Zhishen asked, “Who is this woman? Why is she drinking wine here?” The monk replied, “Brother, allow me to explain. This lady is the daughter of Wang Youjin from the village ahead. Her father was once a patron of this temple, but now the family fortune is exhausted. Of late she has fallen into dire straits: all her household are gone, and her husband is ill, so she came to our temple to borrow rice. For her father’s sake as our former patron, I offered her wine. There is no other intent. Brother, pay no heed to what those old beasts say.” Hearing this account and seeing how deferentially the monk behaved, Zhishen said, “Damn those old monks for making a fool of me!” He lifted his monk’s staff and returned to the temple kitchen. The old monks, having just eaten a little gruel, were still there. Zhishen came out in a fury and, pointing at them, cried, “So it was you fellows who ruined the monastery, yet you still dared lie to my face!” The old monks all cried together, “Brother, do not believe him! Even now he is keeping a woman in there. He saw just now that you carried a戒刀 and monk’s staff, while he had no weapon, so he dared not contend with you. If you do not believe us, go back once more and see how he treats you then. Think for yourself, brother: they feast on wine and meat, while we cannot get even gruel to eat—and just now we were even afraid that you might eat ours.” Zhishen said, “That makes sense too.” Holding his monk’s staff reversed, he returned behind the abbot’s quarters, only to find the side gate already shut. Enraged, Zhishen kicked it open with a single blow and charged inside. There he saw Iron Buddha Cui Daocheng wielding a long-handled saber and rushing out from within to attack him beneath the locust tree. At the sight, Zhishen gave a mighty roar, swung up the monk’s staff in his hands, and engaged Cui Daocheng. They fought for fourteen or fifteen bouts. Unable to match Zhishen, Cui Daocheng could do no more than parry and fend off his blows, twisting aside and dodging the staff. He could not hold out and was just about to flee. Seeing that he could not hold his own, Daoist Qiu seized a long-handled saber and came striding up from behind to thrust at Zhishen. In the midst of the fight, Zhishen suddenly heard footsteps behind him, but dared not turn his head to look.

p.src: Presently he caught sight of a man’s shadow and knew someone meant to ambush him. With a shout of “Take that!” Cui Daocheng panicked, thinking the monk’s staff was coming down on him, and leapt out of the fighting circle with a thud. Only then did Zhishen turn, and the three came face-to-face in a triangular standoff. Cui Daocheng and Daoist Qiu joined forces and fought him for more than another ten bouts. First, Zhishen had nothing in his belly; second, he had traveled a long way; and third, he could not withstand the fresh strength of the two men. He had no choice but to feign an opening, drag away his monk’s staff, and flee. Gripping their long-handled sabers, the two pursued him straight beyond the temple gate. Zhishen fought another ten bouts, then pulled back his staff and fled. The two chased him as far as the stone bridge, then sat on its railing and pursued him no farther.

From afar they resembled a judge of the dead’s whiskers; close at hand, they were just like a demon’s hair. Who had sprinkled fresh blood over the forest boughs? One might think cinnabar had been spread across the treetops.

p.src: Lu Zhishen looked at it and said, “What a fierce and forbidding forest!” As he watched, a man poked his head furtively out from among the shadows of the trees, took one look, spat, and slipped back inside. Zhishen said, “I reckon that scoundrel is a highwayman lying here in wait for prey. When he saw that I was a monk, he thought it a bad omen, spat, and went back in. But the wretch has truly met with ill luck in running into me. My belly is full of cursed anger with nowhere to vent it, so I’ll strip the rascal of his clothes and sell them for wine!” He raised his monk’s staff, rushed straight to the edge of the pine wood, and roared, “Hey, you scoundrel in the forest! Come out at once!” The man heard him from inside the forest and laughed loudly. “What rotten luck! He has come to provoke me instead!” Gripping a broad-bladed sword, he wheeled around and leapt out of the forest, shouting, “Bald donkey! You are seeking your own death—I did not come looking for you!” Zhishen said, “I’ll teach you who I am!” Swinging his monk’s staff, he charged at the man. The man flourished his broad-bladed sword and moved to fight the monk, but just as he was about to advance, he thought, “This monk’s voice sounds very familiar.” He called out, “Hey, monk! Your voice sounds very familiar. What is your surname?” Zhishen replied, “First fight me for three hundred bouts, and then I’ll tell you my name.” The man flew into a rage and met the monk’s staff with the broad-bladed sword in his hands. After they had fought for more than ten bouts, the man secretly applauded him: “What a splendid, ferocious monk!” After another four or five bouts, the man cried, “Hold a moment! I have something to say.” Both leapt out of the fighting circle, and the man asked, “Tell me truly—what is your surname and name? Your voice sounds very familiar.” When Zhishen had given his name, the man cast aside his broad-bladed sword, bowed deeply, and said, “Do you remember Shi Jin?” Zhishen laughed. “So it is Eldest Brother Shi!” They exchanged bows once more, then went into the forest together and sat down. Zhishen asked, “Brother Shi, where have you been since we parted in Weizhou?” Shi Jin replied, “After parting from you outside the tavern that day, I heard the next day that you had beaten Butcher Zheng to death and fled. The officers learned through their inquiries that I had joined you in giving money to old Jin, the singer, so I too left Weizhou and went in search of my master, Wang Jin. I went all the way to Yanzhou, but still could not find him. I returned to the Northern Capital and stayed there for a while, but when my traveling money ran out, I came here to obtain some more. I never expected to meet you. But how did you become a monk?” Zhishen told him the whole story of what had happened, from beginning to end. Shi Jin said, “Since you are hungry, brother, I have some dried meat and baked cakes here.” He took them out and gave them to Zhishen to eat. Shi Jin then said, “Since your bundle is still in the temple, I will go with you to demand it back. If they still refuse, we will finish the wretches off once and for all.” “Right,” said Zhishen. Thereupon he and Shi Jin ate their fill, each took up his weapon, and returned to Crock Temple.

Shi Jin then said, “Since your bundle is still in the temple, I will go with you to demand it back.
If they still refuse, we will finish the wretches off once and for all.”
“Right,” said Zhishen.
Thereupon he and Shi Jin ate their fill, each took up his weapon, and returned to Crock Temple.

p.src: When they reached the front of the temple, they saw Cui Daocheng and Qiu Xiaoyi still sitting on the bridge. Zhishen gave a great roar: “You wretches, come on! This time we shall fight until either you or I lie dead!” The monk laughed. “You were defeated by my hand. How dare you return to fight me again?” Zhishen flew into a rage, swung up his iron monk’s staff, and charged across the bridge. The Iron Buddha, enraged in turn, wielded his broad-bladed sword and rushed down from the bridge. For one thing, having Shi Jin with him had made Zhishen bold at heart; for another, he had eaten his fill, so his vigor and strength flowed forth all the more freely. After eight or nine bouts, Cui Daocheng’s strength gradually failed him, and he thought only of escape; when Qiu Xiaoyi, the Flying Yaksha, saw that the monk was losing, he came to his aid with his broad-bladed sword. On this side, Shi Jin saw him and leapt from the forest, roaring, “None of you shall escape!” He tossed up the brim of his hat, leveled his broad-bladed sword, and engaged Qiu Xiaoyi. The four men fought in two pairs. As Zhishen and Cui Daocheng fought deep into the contest, Zhishen seized an opening and shouted, “Take that!” With a single blow of his monk’s staff, he knocked the Iron Buddha down from the bridge. When the Daoist saw the monk fall, he lost all desire to continue fighting; feigning an opening, he turned and fled. Shi Jin shouted, “Where do you think you’re going?” He caught up and struck the man between the shoulders with his broad-bladed sword. With a heavy thud, the Daoist collapsed to one side. Shi Jin stepped in, reversed his grip on the broad-bladed sword, and thrust it down again and again with ripping, crunching sounds. Zhishen pursued Cui Daocheng below the bridge and struck him from behind with his monk’s staff. Pitiful indeed—the two brigands’ lives dissolved like a dream of Nanke! Just as the saying goes: “All the deeds done in former days bring misfortune at once.” Zhishen and Shi Jin bound the corpses of Qiu Xiaoyi and Cui Daocheng and hurled them into the ravine. The two then forced their way back into the temple. The old monks in the monastery kitchen, having seen Zhishen defeated and fearing that Cui Daocheng and Qiu Xiaoyi would come to kill them, had already hanged themselves. Zhishen and Shi Jin went straight through the rear side gate of the abbot’s quarters and found that the abducted woman had thrown herself into a well and died. They searched as far as eight or nine small rooms within and broke into them, but found no one; they saw only that Zhishen’s bundle had been brought there and had not yet been opened. Lu Zhishen, delighted to recover his bundle, slung it over his back as before. Searching farther inside, they found three or four bundles of clothing on a bed. Shi Jin opened them and found they were all clothes, with some gold and silver wrapped among them. He selected the best pieces, tied them into a bundle, and carried it on his back. They searched the kitchen, found wine and meat, and both ate their fill. Before the stove they bound two torches, raked open the hearth, and lit them from its fire. The flames leapt high, first igniting the small rooms at the rear, then spreading toward the front gate. They bound several more torches, went straight beneath the rear eaves of the Buddha hall, and set it alight. As luck would have it, the wind was strong. The flames roared and crackled until they towered into the sky. Zhishen and Shi Jin watched and waited for a while, until the fire was burning on every side. The two said, “Fine though Prince Liang’s garden may be, it is no place to linger long. We had best be on our way.”

They made their way toward the village and found a tiny tavern beside a single-plank bridge.

p.src: A brushwood gate stood half closed, while a cloth curtain hung low. Jars of sour, thin wine stood by the earthen grove; ink-painted immortals adorned the dusty wall. A village boy measured out the wine—surely no Sima Xiangru washing cups; an ugly woman tended the stove—no Zhuo Wenjun of former days. The bold characters on the wall were inscribed by the village schoolmaster when drunk; the straw raincoat on the rack awaited some country fisherman setting out in high spirits.

p.src: Zhishen and Shi Jin came to an inn in the village. As they drank, they told the waiter to buy some meat and lend them some rice, then lit a fire and cooked a meal. As the two men drank, they told each other of the many things that had happened on the road. When they had finished their wine and food, Zhishen asked Shi Jin, “Where will you go now?” Shi Jin replied, “Now I have no choice but to return to Mount Shaohua, seek refuge with Zhu Wu and the other two, and join their band. I shall stay there for a while and decide what to do afterward.” Hearing this, Zhishen said, “That is indeed what you should do, brother.” He opened his bundle, took out some gold and silver, and gave it to Shi Jin. The two men tied up their bundles, took their weapons, and paid for the wine. They left the inn and the village behind, and after traveling no more than five or seven li, reached a three-way fork. Zhishen said, “Brother, here we must part. I am bound for the Eastern Capital, so do not see me any farther. To reach Huazhou, you must take this road. Someday we shall meet again. If you find a trustworthy traveler, send me word so that we may keep in touch.” Shi Jin bowed farewell to Zhishen, and the two took separate roads. Shi Jin went on his way.

p.src: A thousand gates and ten thousand doors, where vermilion and emerald glittered together; Three markets and six thoroughfares, thronged with finely dressed people. Phoenix pavilions rose in nine tiers of gold and jade; dragon towers displayed ranks of gleaming crystal. Along flowered streets and willow lanes were hosts of celebrated beauties; In the pleasure houses and painted chambers were countless charming singing girls. In mansions of the rich, men gathered to cast dice; noble sons and princes came to purchase smiles.

This is what he saw:

p.src: The mountain gate soared aloft; the temple precincts were serene and secluded. Directly above, the characters on the imperial plaque stood clear; on either side, the guardian kings appeared fierce and mighty. The five-bayed great hall was roofed in orderly rows of green, dragon-scale tiles; The monks’ quarters on all four sides had tortoise-shell-patterned bricks, polished smooth and set in ornamental seams. The bell tower stood solemn and tall; the scripture repository rose majestic. Lofty banner poles reached the blue clouds; the jeweled pagoda seemed to pierce the azure vault of heaven. Wooden fish hung crosswise; cloud-shaped gongs were suspended high. Before the Buddha, lamps and candles shone brilliantly; within the censers, fragrant smoke curled and coiled. Standards and banners stretched without end, from the Guanyin Hall to the Patriarchs’ Hall; Jeweled canopies joined one another, linking the Water-and-Land Assembly hall with the Arhats’ Court. At all times the heavenly guardians descended; year after year the demon-subduing venerable ones came.

p.src: Zhishen entered the monastery, looked along the eastern and western cloisters, and went straight to the guest reception quarters. A lay attendant saw him and reported his arrival to the guest prefect. Before long the guest prefect came out. Seeing Zhishen’s fierce appearance, with an iron monk’s staff in hand, a戒刀 at his waist, and a great bundle on his back, he was already half afraid of him. The guest prefect asked, “From where have you come, brother?” Zhishen set down his bundle and monk’s staff and saluted with joined palms; the guest prefect returned the greeting. Zhishen said, “This humble monk comes from Mount Wutai. My master, Elder Zhizhen, has given me a letter and instructed me to seek refuge here with the venerable Master Zhiqing and ask for a post among the working monks.” The guest prefect said, “Since you bear a letter from the venerable Master Zhizhen, it is proper that we go together to the abbot’s quarters.” The guest prefect led Zhishen straight to the abbot’s quarters. Zhishen opened his bundle, took out the letter, and held it in his hand. The guest prefect said, “Brother, how can you be so ignorant of proper decorum? The elder will be out presently. You must remove your戒刀, take out the seven-strip sitting cloth and an offering of incense, and use them when you bow before him.” Zhishen said, “Why did you not tell me sooner?” He at once removed his戒刀 and took from his bundle a piece of incense and the seven-strip sitting cloth, but for a long while could not work out what to do with them. The guest prefect then helped him put on his kasaya and told him first to spread out the sitting cloth. A little later, Chan Master Zhiqing appeared. The guest prefect stepped forward and reported, “This monk has come from Mount Wutai and bears a letter from Chan Master Zhizhen.” Elder Zhiqing said, “It has been a long time since my brother sent me a letter concerning the Dharma.” The guest prefect called to Zhishen, “Brother, come quickly and bow before the elder.” Zhishen first placed the stick of incense in the censer, bowed three times, and presented the letter. Elder Zhiqing received the letter, opened it, and read the detailed account within: “It explains the circumstances that led Lu Zhishen to enter the monastic life, as well as the reason he has now descended the mountain to seek refuge at your honored monastery; I earnestly beg you, in your compassion, to accept and register him and give him a post among the working monks. On no account find a pretext to refuse him. In time, this monk is certain to attain enlightenment.” After reading the letter, Elder Zhiqing said, “Let the monk who has come from afar go and rest for now in the monks’ hall, and give him a vegetarian meal.” Zhishen thanked him, gathered up the seven-strip sitting cloth, lifted his bundle, took his monk’s staff and戒刀, and followed a young attendant away.

p.src: Elder Zhiqing summoned the many administrative monks of both ranks and gathered them all in the abbot’s quarters. He said, “Now that you monks are all here, see how little sense my brother, Chan Master Zhizhen, has shown. This monk who has come here was originally an officer in the military commandant’s headquarters. Because he beat a man to death, he shaved his head and became a monk. Twice afterward he caused an uproar in the monks’ hall there, so they could no longer keep him. Unable to lodge him at your own monastery, you foist him off on me! —If I refuse to take him in, my brother has entreated me so earnestly, saying, ‘Do not find a pretext to refuse him’; —Yet if I let him stay here and he should disrupt the monastic rules, how could that be allowed?” The guest prefect said, “Indeed, we disciples thought that monk looked nothing at all like a man who had left the secular life. How could this monastery possibly accommodate him?” The monastery administrator then said, “I have been thinking. There is that vegetable garden behind our retirement residence outside the Suanzao Gate. It is constantly being encroached upon by soldiers from the nearby barracks and some twenty local good-for-nothings outside the gate, who turn their sheep and horses loose there and cause endless trouble. An old monk is in charge there, but how would he dare restrain them? Why not send Zhishen to take charge of the place? He might actually be able to keep them under control.” Elder Zhiqing said, “The monastery administrator is right.” He ordered an attendant to wait until Zhishen had finished eating in the guest room of the monks’ hall, and then summon him.

p.src: Before long, the attendant returned and led Zhishen into the abbot’s quarters. Elder Qing said, “Since my senior brother, the Venerable Zhen, recommended you to lodge at this temple and take up an official duty, our humble monastery has a large vegetable garden beyond the Suanzao Gate, beside the Temple of the Sacred Peak. You may go and reside there as its overseer. Each day, have the cultivators deliver ten loads of vegetables; whatever remains shall be yours for expenses.” Zhishen promptly replied, “My master, Elder Zhen, sent this humble monk to your great monastery to obtain a post as an officer-monk. He did not send me to be some prior or steward, perhaps, but how can you tell me to tend a vegetable garden?” The chief seat said, “Brother, you do not understand. You have only just arrived to lodge here and have rendered no service; how could you become prior at once? Overseeing the vegetable garden is already an important office.” Zhishen said, “I won’t tend any vegetable garden. I only want to be prior or steward.” The guest prefect then said, “Listen while I explain. The offices of a Buddhist monastery are divided into various ranks. Take this humble monk’s office of guest prefect: I attend only to visiting lay guests and monks. The precentor, attendant, secretary, and chief seat are all honorable posts, not easily obtained. The prior, steward, superintendent, and bursar all administer the monastery’s common property. You have only just reached the abbot’s quarters; how could you immediately receive a superior office? There is also the keeper of the scriptures, called the canon master; the keeper of the halls, called the hall master; the keeper of the pavilions, called the pavilion master; the one in charge of collecting alms, called the alms master; and the keeper of the bathhouse, called the bath master. These are all supervising officers, posts of the middle rank. Then there are the pagoda keeper, who tends the pagoda; the rice keeper, who manages the meals; the tea keeper, who manages the tea; the privy keeper, who tends the eastern latrine; and the garden keeper, who oversees this vegetable garden. These are all minor functionaries, offices of the lowest rank. Suppose, brother, that you manage the vegetable garden well for a year; then you may be promoted to pagoda keeper. Manage that well for another year, and you may be promoted to bath master. After yet another good year, only then may you become steward.” Zhishen said, “If that is so, there is a path to advancement after all. I’ll go tomorrow.” Seeing that Zhishen had agreed to go, Elder Qing kept him overnight in the abbot’s quarters. That day they settled his appointment, immediately wrote out a public notice, and first sent a man to the garden residence to hang the monastery office’s notice in the quarters vacated by the former incumbent, in readiness for the handover the next day. That night, they all dispersed. Early the next morning, Elder Qing ascended the Dharma seat, endorsed the writ of appointment, and commissioned Zhishen to oversee the vegetable garden. Zhishen came before the seat, received the writ, took leave of the elder, slung his bundle over his back, strapped on his戒刀, picked up his monk’s staff, and, accompanied by two monks sent to install him, went straight to the residence beyond the Suanzao Gate to take up his post. Early the next morning, Elder Qing ascended the Dharma seat, endorsed the writ of appointment, and commissioned Zhishen to oversee the vegetable garden.

Zhishen came before the seat, received the writ, took leave of the elder, slung his bundle over his back, strapped on his戒刀, picked up his monk’s staff, and, accompanied by two monks sent to install him, went straight to the residence beyond the Suanzao Gate to take up his post.
A poem says:

p.src: A drifting wanderer enters the Eastern Capital, having crossed forests and mountains for scores of stages. This ancient monastery shall now pass through consuming fire; from this moment, weapons of war shall stir throughout the Central Plain. At the Xiangguo Temple he lodges anew, and for now tends the vegetable garden. Since ancient times, white clouds have known neither going nor staying; through countless transformations they roam at will.

p.src: Now, near the vegetable garden lived twenty or thirty shiftless gamblers, ruined idlers, and local rogues, who habitually stole vegetables from the garden to support themselves. When they came to steal vegetables, they saw a new notice from the monastery office posted on the residence gate. It read: “The Great Xiangguo Temple hereby appoints the monk Lu Zhishen to reside here and oversee the vegetable garden. Beginning tomorrow, he shall take charge, and no unauthorized persons shall be permitted to enter the garden and cause disturbances.” After reading it, several rogues went to consult the other idlers, saying, “The Great Xiangguo Temple has sent some monk named Lu Zhishen to oversee the vegetable garden. While he is still new, let us pick a quarrel, give him a sound beating, and make the fellow submit to us.” One of their number said, “I have a plan. He has never met us, so how can we simply go and start a quarrel? When he arrives, we’ll lure him to the edge of the cesspit, pretending that we have come to pay our respects. Then we’ll seize both his feet, flip him head over heels, and pitch the fellow into the cesspit. It will be only a little joke at his expense.” The rogues all cried, “Good! Good!” Their plan settled, they waited for him to come.

p.src: Meanwhile, Lu Zhishen reached the quarters in the vacated residence, settled his bundle and luggage in the inner room, propped up his monk’s staff, and hung up his戒刀. The several lay brothers who worked the land all came to pay their respects, and every key and lock in their charge was duly handed over. The two monks took leave of the old monk who had formerly held the post, and all returned to the temple. Zhishen then went out into the vegetable garden, looking east and west as he inspected the grounds. Presently he saw the twenty or thirty rogues carrying boxes of fruit and gifts of wine. All smiles, they said, “We heard that the reverend has newly come to take charge, so we neighbors from the surrounding streets have come to congratulate you.” Zhishen, unaware of their scheme, walked straight to the edge of the cesspit. The band of rogues surged forward together: one seized his left foot and another his right, intending to topple Zhishen. Yet wherever Zhishen’s toes rose, even a fierce tiger before the mountain would tremble in fear; and wherever his fists descended, dragons throughout the seas would lose their courage. Indeed, this quiet, ordinary garden was now drawn up as a little battlefield. As for how that band of rogues tried to topple Zhishen, listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
